_note: Single source of truth for the asset log page. Nothing on public/log/index.html is hand-written — run `npm run log` to regenerate, `npm run log:check` to catch drift. Add a revision here, not in the HTML.

page.sub: The living record of one study: a set of scroll-driven WebGL forms built out of formulas instead of 3D models. Every asset in this repo, how it was made, every time it changed, and who asked for the change. Dead ends included.

premise.claim: You can reach a convincing 3D asset without authoring any geometry, if the treatment carries it.
premise.status: held — and confirmed by the director
premise.scope: Now tested well past one form on black: a scroll-driven page carrying three particle systems, frosted glass panels with footage behind them, and one shared light, all without an engine. Lee's verdict: "this is proving we dont need to run the webgl and three js through a engine." Still untested on a multi-page site, which is the next thing and is not a rendering question.

rules.rule: Free assets are clay, not the final look.
rules.why: A downloaded mesh with its default texture reads as a free mesh. The expensive feeling comes from lighting, grade, material, motion and post — the layers we control. Skip that and you get asset soup.

rules.rule: Treatment belongs to the asset, not the page.
rules.why: Learned the hard way on Ocellus. A four-panel rig that flatters a knot reflects off a sphere as grey rectangles. Every catalogue entry now carries its own light AND post recipe, and can opt out of the base rig entirely.

rules.rule: Every aesthetic knob goes on a slider.
rules.why: Taste is superb at picking and tuning and terrible at describing. Wiring the knobs to Leva means the director's eye drives the pixels directly instead of the subtlety having to survive translation into adjectives. Variant grids for the same reason — selection is effortless where specification is agony.
Anything placed by a random draw gets a seeded PRNG. An asset that rolls a different lottery on every refresh cannot be art-directed — you would be tuning a thing that no longer exists.
No example imports from another. helixCurve.js is duplicated on purpose rather than shared, so any folder can be copied out whole. Local assets only — no CDN fonts, no remote HDRI.

rules.rule: Instrument rather than guess on performance.
rules.why: The browser these are built through renders on the CPU, so no framerate number from the build process would mean anything. So the page measures itself on whatever GPU it lands on, adapts its own pixel ratio, and exposes every expensive knob. The stats panel is the only real evidence.

rules.rule: Check shader geometry numerically, not just by eye.
rules.why: A still frame cannot show orbit, containment or wrap, and those are exactly the properties that go quietly wrong. Re-run the shader maths on the CPU and assert the population-level claims. It is cheap, it runs without a GPU, and here it caught particles rendering inside the glass after the picture had already been signed off four times.

rules.rule: One light direction, exported from one place.
rules.why: Every part of a scene that draws a pixel has to agree about where the light is — the environment, the lamps, any baked vertex shading, and every particle shader. Four separate answers is how a scene ends up looking lit from nowhere. Elevation and azimuth on sliders, one vector derived from them, consumed everywhere.

rules.rule: Shared behaviour lives in shared code.
rules.why: When two things are specified to move the same way, put the motion in one module both consume. Copies satisfy the requirement once and then diverge silently under tuning — nothing errors, they just stop agreeing, and the drift is invisible until someone notices the scene looks wrong.

rules.rule: Verify a backup by restoring it.
rules.why: Writing the file proves the write succeeded and nothing else. Clone the bundle, extract the archive, compare against the original, and record how to do it next to the files. A restore point discovered to be bad at the moment it is needed is worse than none, because it was counted on.

rules.rule: Prove a check can fail before trusting it to pass.
rules.why: A test that has only ever returned the answer you wanted might be measuring nothing. Run it against a case known to be positive first. Here a wrong element id reported a control panel absent in both the build that hid it and the build that showed it.

rules.rule: A living page names its own project in its heading.
rules.why: One page per project, and it has to say which — the h1 carries the project, the document type sits above it as a kicker. A page led by its document type cannot be told apart from every other page built in the same format. Checked rather than remembered: the build fails when the project field is missing, when it matches a blocklist of generic document nouns, or when the rendered heading doesn't contain it.

rules.rule: Let the material do the effect.
rules.why: Before reaching for a filter, check whether something already in the scene produces it physically. Content placed behind glass is diffused by the glass, and that diffusion cannot drift out of step with the material the way a hand-matched blur would.

One video per card means one decoder per card, and five running at once is how a page like this stutters on a laptop. Play inside a radius wider than the fade, so a panel is already running by the time it can be seen, and pause everything else.

rules.rule: Stop adding before it is obvious you should have.
rules.why: Each effect here was justified on its own and the page still filled up. Nothing in the build tells you when to stop, because every individual addition renders correctly and looks defensible in isolation. Density is a decision made about the whole page, from outside it.

rules.rule: Fit both axes, at the depth the content actually sits.
rules.why: Solving a camera distance for one dimension leaves the other to the aspect ratio, and the failure only appears at ratios away from the one being worked at. Ask each piece of content how far back the camera must be for it, at its own depth, and take the largest answer.

assets.name: Knot
assets.line: Parametric torus knot in transmission glass.
assets.made_of: One line of JSX. torusKnotGeometry(1, 0.32, 220, 32) in a MeshTransmissionMaterial, lit by four Lightformers arranged key / rim / rim / fill, over a near-black ground, with bloom and a vignette on top. The smoothness is tessellation, and it costs nothing because the form is generated from a formula rather than stored and loaded. This asset is the whole argument in one object: it was mistaken for a modeled mesh, and there is no mesh.

recipe.backside: off — the most expensive checkbox here
recipe.spin: 0.15 rad/s on Y, 0.35× that on X

revisions.change: Built as 001-glass-hero, a single hero form, plus a look-tuning pass.
revisions.why: Wanted as a smoke test for the freshly-scaffolded repo. Also an overreach — see A-02; it was kept rather than deleted.

revisions.change: 001-glass-hero → 001-glass-catalogue. The number was preserved; only the descriptor changed. Knot became one entry of three behind a browse strip.
revisions.why: Once a second asset existed, a page called 'hero' was lying about what it was. The number is a rung on the capability ladder, so renumbering would have been the wrong fix.

revisions.change: Added a shape selector — torus knot / icosahedron / torus / box — on the same material.
revisions.why: Cheapest possible demonstration that the material and rig, not the form, are doing the work.

revisions.change: Scoped every Leva control folder per asset.
revisions.why: Leva persists control values by path, not by component lifetime, so remounting on a catalogue switch did not reset anything — and the per-asset defaults each entry carried were silently doing nothing. Noticed here because the Knot is the first asset the switcher lands on.

revisions.change: backside off by default, transmission resolution 512 → 256, composer multisampling 8 → 2.
revisions.why: backside renders the mesh a second time through the transmission pass. The transmission material re-renders the whole scene into a buffer every frame, so halving its resolution is a quarter of the pixels. Arithmetic reductions in work, not measured framerate gains — see L-13.

assets.name: Ocellus
assets.line: A radial iris suspended in a glass orb. Instanced fibres, deterministic.
assets.made_of: An eye with nothing modeled in it. A dark disc for the sclera, a torus for the limbal ring, a black circle for the pupil, about 220 instanced boxes fanned out radially as iris fibres, and a sphere of glass over the whole thing. The orb's refraction magnifies and bends the fibres behind it, and that bending is what actually sells it as an eye — not the parts list. Fibre placement runs off a seeded PRNG so it is identical on every load.

recipe.fibres: ~220 instanced boxes, radial fan, seeded PRNG
recipe.orb: thin transmission sphere, no nested transmission inside it
recipe.light: base rig OFF entirely; round catchlights only

revisions.change: Built as the second catalogue entry, to test whether the premise survived a form with internal structure rather than a single solid.
revisions.why: A knot is the friendliest possible case. An eye has parts that have to read through each other.

revisions.change: First version rendered almost entirely black.
revisions.why: Glass shows you what is behind it, and behind it was a dark interior on a dark background — so the transmission sphere absorbed everything. Fixed by making the iris emit its own light and thinning the orb. Adding more lights would not have worked; the problem was that there was nothing to see through to.

revisions.change: Iris fibres were originally a transmission material too, sitting inside the orb's transmission pass. Replaced with clearcoat + iridescence.
revisions.why: Each transmission material forces its own full-scene render. Nesting them tanked the frame hard enough that headless screenshots timed out. The fibres read as glass anyway, because the orb in front is doing the real refracting.

revisions.change: Opted out of the shared four-panel light rig; lit by its own round catchlights instead.
revisions.why: Big rectangular lightformers reflect off a sphere as literal grey rectangles and read as CG instantly. Circular formers are most of what makes an eye look wet. This is the revision that produced rule R-02.

revisions.change: Fibre placement moved from Math.random to a seeded PRNG.
revisions.why: The asset was rolling a different arrangement on every refresh. You cannot art-direct a lottery — you would be tuning something that will not exist next reload.

assets.name: Strand
assets.line: A double helix of glass pipe with 12,000 particles running through it.
assets.geometry: two tubeGeometry sweeps along an analytic helix, merged — particles positioned in a vertex shader
assets.made_of: The helix is a formula, which is the important part: the same three lines drive the tube sweep on the CPU and every particle position in the vertex shader, so they cannot drift out of sync and nothing is updated per frame. Both strands are merged into a single geometry so there is one transmission pass instead of two. 12,000 particles ride through the pipe like water, over a dimmer inner tube of additive colour that gives the flow a body.

recipe.particles: 12,000, positioned entirely in a vertex shader
recipe.strands: 2, merged into one geometry → one transmission pass
recipe.flow body: inner additive tube under the points
recipe.ior: dropped from 1.44 — see the stripes failure below

revisions.change: Built as the third catalogue entry — a form plus a flow, rather than a form alone.
revisions.why: The first two assets are objects. This one tests whether motion through a form can be carried procedurally too.

revisions.change: The particle flow went through five versions before it worked. Bright and dense it swamped the glass and looked like glowing rope; small and sparse it looked like dirt in a tube.
revisions.why: The fix was structural rather than numeric, which is why four rounds of tuning numbers got nowhere. Real fluid has a luminous body, so there is now a dimmer inner tube of additive colour with the particles riding on top as detail. Particles alone read as dust.

revisions.change: At ior 1.44 the tube facets bent the particles behind them into hard diagonal bands that read as scales on a snake. Dropped the index.
revisions.why: Glass that refracts hard is beautiful over an empty background and ruinous over something you want to see. The lower index makes it behave like a clear shell rather than a lens.

revisions.change: Bloom threshold lowered to 0.42 for this asset specifically.
revisions.why: The threshold of 0.9 that keeps the Knot's glass clean swallowed the emissive particles entirely. Second piece of evidence for R-02 — post belongs to the asset too, not just lighting.

revisions.change: Merged tube geometries are now disposed when parameters change.
revisions.why: They were rebuilt by useMemo on every parameter change and the old buffers were never freed, so dragging a slider leaked GPU memory until the tab was closed. A real bug, found while doing something else.

assets.name: Strand (scroll variant)
assets.line: The same helix held still in world space while a camera travels along it.
assets.geometry: tubeGeometry along the same analytic helix, 60 units long — camera travels 42 of them
assets.made_of: A deliberate inversion of Strand: there, the form rotates and the flow is driven by time. Here the form does not move at all and the camera does the travelling, because 'a card every so often along it' needs a distance to measure against. The particle flow accumulator became flow += delta * (drift + |scrollVelocity| * surge) — the swap from a time uniform to scroll progress was about three lines, exactly as predicted when the concept was pressure-tested.

recipe.cards: real DOM <a> anchors, world position projected to screen each frame
recipe.card fade: opacity, pointer-events and tabIndex all follow camera distance
recipe.camera distance: fitted on both axes: the larger of the width fit and, per piece of content, (reach + margin) / tan(fov/2) + that content's depth
recipe.visible span: also scaled by aspect, clamp 0.4–1.0 — the portrait mitigation
recipe.tessellation: segmentsPerTurn exposed — a long helix multiplies segments by turns
recipe.lighting: one direction (elevation/azimuth) shared by the environment, a directional lamp, the core's baked vertex shading and both particle shaders

revisions.change: Built as the scroll capability test — the last real unknown before committing to a direction.
revisions.why: Four questions in order of doubt: does scroll-driven camera work in this stack, does 'alive at rest' actually feel different, can cards be real links, does the responsive strategy hold. Three came back clean on the first build; the fourth is the failure below.

revisions.change: First version computed camera distance so a chosen world-width always fit the frame. Correct on desktop; on portrait it pushed the camera so far back the helix became a thread in a void. Mitigated by scaling the visible span with aspect too.
revisions.why: Technically correct framing, visually dead. The mitigation takes portrait from broken to acceptable, NOT to good — a horizontal form in a tall frame wastes most of the screen however it is scaled. The honest fix is a rotated vertical variant designed as its own composition, and it is not built. This is the most useful negative result in the log.

revisions.change: Moved the full-screen scroll proxy before the interactive layers in the DOM, and put the wheel listener on window rather than on the scroller.
revisions.why: The proxy sat over the cards and swallowed every click. And with the listener on the scroller, scrolling died whenever the cursor was over a card.

revisions.change: Adaptive pixel ratio (0.75–2.0) via a performance monitor, replacing a fixed [1, 2]. Tube tessellation exposed. Live stats panel behind perf → stats.
revisions.why: Cost scales with the square of pixel ratio, so 2.0 → 1.5 is 44% fewer pixels shaded. The ratio walks itself up when frames are cheap and down when they are not, so a big desktop GPU and a laptop integrated chip both land somewhere sensible without a device check.

revisions.change: Gained a second particle system orbiting outside the glass. The form itself is unchanged.
revisions.why: The scroll velocity that already drove the flow inside the tube turned out to be enough to drive something outside it too, in a different way — the same input reused rather than a new one added.

revisions.change: The particle geometry here leaked on every count change — the same undisposed-useMemo bug that was found and fixed in the tube during the perf pass, still present one file over.
revisions.why: The original fix was applied where the bug was found rather than everywhere the pattern occurred, so it survived. Noticed only because the new veil needed the same disposal and the neighbouring file was open.

revisions.change: Lighting pass across the whole scene. One shared direction on elevation/azimuth sliders now drives the environment strips, a directional lamp, half-lambert vertex colours baked into the luminous core, and the shading in both particle shaders. The underside fill dropped from 2.2 against a 4.5 key to a weak cold bounce; glass roughness up from 0.04 with clearcoat added, so the key returns as a travelling streak instead of a pinpoint.
revisions.why: Lee called the whole thing flat, and it was — but not for the reason it looked like. The glass was fine. The scene was lit four separate ways that did not agree, and the strong underside fill removed the dark side that a form needs in order to read as a shape at all.

revisions.change: Made fit to share. The tuning panel now only appears while developing or behind ?tune, a one-line hint tells an arriving visitor the page moves sideways and disappears the moment they touch anything, the title and description read as something rather than as a build artefact, and a preview image means a shared link unfurls with a picture. The same still serves as the gallery thumbnail.
revisions.why: The page had been live since the first push, so nothing needed deploying — what it needed was to stop assuming its visitor had built it. The panel-hiding was then verified twice, because the first check used an element id the library does not use and would have reported success either way.

revisions.change: The log now leads with the project's name and demotes 'Asset log' to a kicker above it, and a card in the scene links straight here instead of by way of the index. Three new build checks: the project must be named, the name must not be a generic document noun, and the rendered heading must contain it.
revisions.why: Content was never the problem — every asset here is this repo's and the only outbound link is this repo. The page simply never said whose it was, which beside another project's page in the same format is enough to blur the two. All three checks were confirmed to fire against seeded failures before being trusted.

revisions.change: The camera fits both axes. Width alone made the distance inversely proportional to the aspect ratio, so wide screens pulled the camera in and cut the panels off — measured at -0.38 units of clearance on a 2:1 monitor and -0.58 on a phone held sideways. Both now clear by the stated margin, and portrait is untouched because the width fit still wins there.
revisions.why: Reported from real hardware with screenshots, which is the only place it could have come from: every frame this study was ever reviewed in was 640x400 or 900x560, and both sit near the one aspect where the bug almost does not show.

assets.name: Dust
assets.line: A sheath of very small motes orbiting the form's own long axis — coherent when driven, turbulent when let go, and occasionally catching the light.
assets.geometry: 40k points on a cylindrical shell around the X axis, positioned entirely in the vertex shader
assets.made_of: Stateless, on the same principle as the flow inside the tube: a particle's position is a pure function of its seed and four accumulators, so the whole veil costs four uniform writes a frame. Orbiting around the long axis rather than drifting past is what makes it cross in front of the glass and then behind it — the veil has to cross the form or it just sits beside it. About 30% of the particles orbit the opposite way so the cloud churns through itself instead of turning like a wheel. Scroll velocity feeds two separate accumulators: one adds swirl, the other drags the whole population along the axis, wrapped so it can never be emptied out.

recipe.shell: inner and depth both expressed as multiples of the glass's OUTER surface (radius + tube), never the centreline
recipe.radial bias: shell fraction ** 1.6 — densest against the glass, thinning outward
recipe.axial drag: drift += delta × scrollVelocity × follow, signed, per-particle drag 0.55–1.45 so it shears instead of sliding as a block
recipe.two states: a calm term eased toward 1 - min(1, |velocity| × 2.5); every turbulence term is multiplied by it
recipe.turbulence: three out-of-phase sine terms, not curl noise — nobody can resolve a single path at this size, only the aggregate
recipe.billow: displaces the shell FRACTION, reflected at both ends, so radius cannot leave the sheath whatever the noise does
recipe.sprite: broad gaussian, exp(-d²×12) minus the value at the rim so the discard leaves no visible edge
recipe.wrap: fract() on the axial coordinate, with the outer eighth at each end faded out to hide the seam
recipe.lighting: half-lambert against the shared light direction, ambient floor so the shadow side scatters rather than going dead black
recipe.sparkle: facet term (half-vector, tightness 18) x per-particle flicker (sin^26) x a 14% reflective subset; a glinting mote also grows ~90%

revisions.change: Built as a second particle system around the scroll form, orbiting the long axis, with the two-state behaviour the ask describes: streaming and coherent under scroll, turbulent and wandering at rest.
revisions.why: Everything in the study so far was either always-moving or driven-only. A form whose character depends on whether it is currently being pushed is a different thing, and it is the first time the scroll input has been used for anything other than speed.

revisions.change: First version read as a starfield rather than smoke. Two causes: the default size put every point at about a quarter of a pixel, so it clamped to a hard dot and the soft falloff never ran; and the falloff was cubed, which concentrated the alpha into the sprite centre where the bloom pass then picked it out as a spark.
revisions.why: Both came from taking “very small particles” literally in world units without working out what it meant in pixels at the camera distance the scene actually uses. Recorded because the picture looked deliberate — an even field of fine points is a plausible-looking wrong answer, which is the kind that survives review.

revisions.change: The veil was rendering partly inside the glass. Its inner radius was a multiple of the helix centreline radius and ignored the tube's own thickness, putting the floor 0.13 units inside the wall; the billow term then scaled that radius and could push a particle a further 22% inward, down to 1.03 against a wall at 1.45. Fixed by measuring clearance from radius + tube, and by making billow displace the shell fraction — reflected at both ends — so the radius is structurally unable to leave the sheath.
revisions.why: Neither bug was visible in a still frame, and four rounds of looking at screenshots had already passed them. They were found by re-running the vertex shader on the CPU and asserting the properties directly. The containment is now a property of how the radius is constructed rather than something the noise settings have to be careful not to break.

revisions.change: Fourteen knobs exposed — shell geometry, orbit rate and scroll surge, axial follow, counter-rotating fraction, turbulence, billow, wander, and how fast it settles after the scroll stops.
revisions.why: Whether this reads as smoke or as fine dust is a judgement nobody can make from a description, and it has to be made on a real GPU at full resolution. The defaults are a starting point, not an answer.

revisions.change: Renamed from Veil to Dust after Lee judged it on real hardware: it reads as fine dust, not smoke. Kept as a deliberate choice rather than a failed one.
revisions.why: It was built to be smoke and it is not smoke. Renaming it is the honest move and it also changes what to do next — dust is discrete motes that catch light individually, which is a thing to lean into rather than blur away. The asset id stays 'smoke-veil' because this log is a record of how it got here, not a tidy-up.

revisions.change: Motes are lit by the shared light direction, and a subset of them sparkle. 14% are reflective at all; a half-vector facet term decides where a glint is possible and a per-particle flicker decides when, so roughly 98 of 40,000 are glinting at any instant, all on the lit side.
revisions.why: Dust that does not catch the light is just noise on the frame. Splitting the sparkle into a 'where' and a 'when' is what stops it reading as the whole field blinking — verified numerically rather than by eye, because a still frame catches an arbitrary instant of an intermittent effect.

revisions.change: Rebuilt on the shared orbit module. Behaviour unchanged — the motion is the same code it always was, now in one place instead of about to become two.
revisions.why: A second system was specified to move identically. Extracting rather than copying was the only version of that which survives either one being tuned later.

assets.name: Flakes
assets.line: Rare, much larger hexagonal plates riding the same orbit as the dust, tumbling like falling snow and flashing iridescent when a face catches the light.
assets.geometry: 220 instanced flat hexagons (a 6-segment circle), oriented per-instance in the vertex shader
assets.made_of: The one thing in the sheath with a face. Everything else here is a point sprite, which is always square-on to the camera and can therefore only brighten; a plate can turn, and turning is what lets it catch the light, sweep colour and vanish edge-on. It rides the identical orbit as the dust — literally the same GLSL and the same update function, pulled out into a shared module, because 'behaves the same way' is a requirement that two copies would quietly break. The tumble runs on its own clock rather than the orbit's: snow keeps turning at the same lazy rate whether or not it is being blown along.

recipe.orbit: shared with the dust, same module, same parameters
recipe.tumble: two angles at unrelated per-plate rates plus a flutter term; no shared period, so no visible loop
recipe.measured tumble: ~38s per full turn; fastest plate 12x the slowest
recipe.basis: reference vector swaps when the normal nears vertical, or the cross product collapses once per tumble
recipe.lighting: lit by its own face, not by where it sits on the shell — a plate underneath with its face turned up really is catching the key
recipe.edge-on: alpha scales with how square-on the plate is to the viewer, so it thins to nothing sideways
recipe.shine: abs(dot(normal, half)) ^ 16 — abs because a flake is thin enough that either face can take the light
recipe.iridescence: three offset cosines driven by the viewing angle; carried at a base level at all times and pushed to full by a flash, so the colour does not depend on catching the light
recipe.measured flash: ~11 of 220 plates flashing at any instant, each one lit ~2% of the time

revisions.change: Built as the third element in the sheath — rare, several times larger than the dust, tumbling slowly, flashing iridescent when a face lines up with the light.
revisions.why: The ask needed something a point sprite cannot do. Verified numerically the way the rest of the sheath has been: the basis never degenerates over 400 simulated seconds, the tumble is slow and never repeats, both faces flash, and plates genuinely pass through edge-on. A still frame can show none of that.

revisions.change: Pulled the orbital motion out of the dust into a shared module and rebuilt both systems on it, rather than copying the shader into the new one.
revisions.why: 'They behave the same way as the dust' is a requirement. A copy satisfies it on the first day and breaks it silently the first time either is tuned — nothing errors, the two just stop agreeing. Sharing the code makes it structural.

revisions.change: Split the hue from the flash. Colour was previously mixed in by the flash term alone, so between flashes the plates were grey and only the few currently catching the light had any iridescence at all. A base level now carries the tint independently and the flash adds brightness over it. Defaults raised with it: more plates, higher opacity, a wider flash.
revisions.why: Lee preferred a render that had been over-driven purely to demonstrate the mechanism. The literal reading — widen the flash until everything flashes — would have bought the colour back by destroying the event the flash represents. The preference was pointing at the grey between flashes, which was a fault rather than a setting.

assets.name: Panels
assets.line: Large frosted glass slabs standing forward of the form, carrying the navigation and overlapping the helix without hiding it.
assets.geometry: 5 extruded rounded rectangles with bevelled edges, merged into one geometry, plus a separate flat ring for the rim
assets.made_of: Half WebGL and half DOM, on purpose. The panel is an extruded rounded rectangle with a bevel — the bevel is most of why it reads as a slab rather than a decal, since it gives the rim a surface at an angle to the face that can pick up the key and bend what is behind it. The label stays a real DOM anchor sitting on top, because that was this example's actual finding and it is not worth trading for a material. All five panels are merged into ONE geometry: the transmission material re-renders the whole scene into a buffer every frame, so five separate panels would have meant five extra full scene renders per frame on top of the one the tube already costs.

recipe.size: 3.6 x 2.1, lifted 1.35 above or below the axis, standing at z 1.75
recipe.overlap: the lift is small enough that the panel covers the near half of the form and lets the rest read around it
recipe.edge: drawn as its own additive ring just proud of the front face, because clear glass on black has nothing to reflect and is found by its edges first
recipe.surface: roughness 0.28 with a procedural grain map — fine noise plus a low-frequency vertical streak, generated on a canvas, no external asset
recipe.depth ordering: panels write depth, so the flakes orbiting out to ~3.9 cross in front of a face standing at 1.75 now and then, which was the point
recipe.placement: x and side are fixed per card; the world position is derived once and consumed by both the glass and the DOM anchor, so they cannot drift apart

revisions.change: Built as glass behind the existing DOM cards rather than as a replacement for them. Panels stand forward of the form, overlap it without hiding it, and keep the alternating above/below placement.
revisions.why: The cards were the thing this example proved. Rebuilding them in WebGL would have bought real refraction by giving back keyboard navigation, screen readers, indexable text and browser-rendered type. Putting the glass behind the anchor keeps both results at one stated cost.

revisions.change: First version was invisible. Physically correct glass — transmission 1, low roughness, real thickness — on a near-black background reflects nothing, so the panel could only be located by the smear it made of the form behind it.
revisions.why: Found by swapping in an opaque debug material, which showed the panel exactly where it should be, at the right size, correctly aligned with its label. The geometry was never wrong; the scene gave the material nothing to return. Fixed by drawing the edge as real geometry and frosting the face enough to scatter the key across it.

assets.name: Screens
assets.line: A different loop behind every panel, kept distant by the glass in front of it, throwing raked light forward through it.
assets.geometry: one plane per panel behind the glass, plus a 22-slice beam in front of each; both merged into single geometries
assets.made_of: Two pieces that only make sense together. The screen is never drawn sharp and is never blurred either — the panel in front is frosted and its transmission pass diffuses whatever is behind it, so the material does the work and the setback distance is the whole distance control. The beam is a stack of soft slices lying in the plane the camera always faces, marching along a raked axis and coloured, six times a second, by the average colour of the footage at that moment. One video element feeds all five panels, each taking a different crop of the same frame.

recipe.diffusion: none applied — the panel's own transmission pass does it; setback is the distance knob
recipe.clearance: the screen must stay outside 1.45 from the axis or it pokes through the form
recipe.distance: desaturation rather than dimming — colour goes before light does
recipe.beam: 22 slices in the XY plane, which in this scene is camera-facing because the camera travels but never turns
recipe.rake: blended from the scene's own light direction — light leaves a window travelling away from what lit it, and an unraked beam is seen down its own axis and has no length
recipe.striation: two incommensurate frequencies across the beam; without it an unbroken rectangle emits a wash
recipe.colour: sampled from a 1x1 canvas draw of the video, 6 times a second — the browser's own downscale is the averaging
recipe.fade: beams and screens fade with camera distance the same way the labels do, or every panel sprays light at once
recipe.decoders: one per card, playing only inside a radius wider than the fade
recipe.placeholder: public/media/panel-loop.mp4 — 39KB, generated, seamless palindrome loop; swap the src for real footage
recipe.sources: five 1.3-4.2s loops cut from the Blender Foundation's open movies (CC BY 3.0), 284KB total; credits in public/media/ATTRIBUTION.md
recipe.looping: seamless by crossfading the tail onto the head, not by palindrome — a palindrome reads as rewind on character animation
recipe.transparency: normal blending under full opacity, plus a luma key that holds back the dark end; additive is available and is not the default

revisions.change: Footage behind the panels and light thrown forward through them. Ships with a generated abstract loop as a stand-in.
revisions.why: The study needed a reason to keep going rather than only something to look at. The placeholder is generated rather than sourced because this repo is public and carries no media it did not make.

revisions.change: The beams went wrong twice. First as a hollow frustum lit by a rim term, which drew two hard diagonal lines across the frame — the geometry's own outline rather than light. Then, once softened into slices, as an even wash with no ray structure at all.
revisions.why: Two different mistakes with the same root: treating a beam as a surface. A rim term is right for a shell standing in for an atmosphere and wrong for an open cone. And rays are only legible because something breaks the source up — a plain rectangle emits evenly, so the striation had to be put in deliberately.

revisions.change: A different loop per card, cut from open-licensed animation, with per-card decoders that only run near the camera and a transparency that keeps the picture.
revisions.why: One shared clip across five panels was the cheap version and it read as five copies of one thing. The three things that went wrong are all recorded above: additive blending was the obvious answer to 'see-through' and was wrong at the bright end, the decoders doubled because a DOM append sat inside a useMemo, and the first cut of the clips came back full of title cards because nobody looked at the footage first.

asks.summary: Set the strategy before any code: no custom engine, procedural and shader-driven as the primary lane, free assets are clay, communicate by direct manipulation rather than verbal specification.
asks.effect: Everything in this log follows from here. The rules panel is this decision, unpacked.

asks.verbatim: I only wanted you to make the repos. I didnt ask you to make an example.
asks.summary: Scope correction. Repos had been asked for; an example and a look-tuning pass were delivered on top, unasked.
asks.effect: Stopped mid-turn, reported state, offered to delete it. Kept as a smoke test — which is how the Knot exists. The standing lesson: when infrastructure is asked for, infrastructure is what is meant. The creative content is the director's seat.

asks.verbatim: that shape was impressive... the lighting was excellent
asks.summary: Asked whether a newer model had brought some new 3D capability with it.
asks.effect: Corrected honestly: it is torusKnotGeometry(1, 0.32, 220, 32), a built-in parametric primitive with zero authored geometry. The look came from the treatment. Not a new capability — an old principle working.

asks.summary: Turn the single hero into a browsable catalogue of named assets, referable by stable id.
asks.effect: 001-glass-hero → 001-glass-catalogue; Ocellus and Strand built; ids fixed so a brief can name an asset without ambiguity. Names and tuning stay changeable, ids do not.

asks.summary: Naming convention: NNN-technique-descriptor, with the searchable detail in a per-example meta.json.
asks.effect: Number is a rung on the capability ladder, technique is the one thing demonstrated, descriptor is flavour. Folder name for scanning, meta for finding. The gallery builds itself from those files; a scaffold script enforces the convention.

asks.verbatim: you are able to mimic 3d assets with code, and the combination of those assets with particle effects and lighting can be made spectacular... So i think we can make my vision without using actual 3d assets.
asks.summary: Verdict on the three assets. The premise held.
asks.effect: Closed the largest open risk in the project — bespoke 3D asset creation was the identified long pole and it stopped being a blocker. Tempered at the time: the work did not shrink, the bottleneck moved from modeling into maths and shader craft. Relocated effort, not less of it.

asks.summary: Described the working concept: a horizontally-scrolling page, a double helix that does not move, only the particles moving and driven by scroll, cards along it acting as the navigation.
asks.effect: Pressure-tested as a strong fit — every element is a formula, nothing needs modeling. The specific strength named at the time: the structure holds still and only the flow moves, which is the cheapest thing to animate and among the most beautiful. Geometry gets built once and never touched.

asks.verbatim: a beautiful scroll on one screen sucks on another
asks.summary: Raised responsiveness as a first-class risk before anything was built.
asks.effect: Produced the responsive strategy — normalised 0→1 progress decoupled from pixels, length as a multiple of viewport, camera distance from aspect, cards as DOM over the canvas, and portrait rotating rather than shrinking. Half of it was then confirmed empirically and half of it failed; see L-10 and L-11. This ask paid for itself.

asks.summary: The organising principle for the whole responsive problem.
asks.effect: If the user never sees a whole object, there is no wrong crop — so the problem partly dissolves rather than being solved. Helix ends stay off-frame, breakpoint variants never co-occur, there are no section cuts, cards ease in rather than pop. Also surfaced the one seam with an architectural consequence: the page transition. Noted as a misread of 'scenes' at the time, and the real phrase was the better idea.

asks.summary: Greenlit the scroll capability test — explicitly after it had been offered rather than started.
asks.effect: 002-scroll-helix. Three of four questions came back clean; the fourth produced the portrait failure, which is the most valuable thing in this log.

asks.verbatim: we will worry about the perf pass later, but dont forget we need to worry about it
asks.summary: Deferred performance without dropping it, then later chose the perf pass over the vertical variant and the persistent-canvas test.
asks.effect: Adaptive pixel ratio, cheaper transmission defaults, backside off, multisampling down, a live stats toggle — and a GPU memory leak found and fixed along the way. Approach forced by L-13: measurement was impossible from the build environment, so the answer was to instrument rather than guess.

asks.summary: Asked for this page — a living log of the assets, how they were made, how they changed, and the asks that changed them.
asks.effect: This document. Generated from a manifest so it cannot quietly go stale, and the protocol for keeping it current is now a standing rule of the project rather than something to remember.

asks.verbatim: I need a particle smoke, very small paticles, that appear to surround the double helix and orbit it around the enteral axis of the helix, and as I scroll the smoke swirls around the outside of the helix and follows the scrolling. When not scrolling, it should become more random swirling, rom front to back and back to front, around the central axis of the double helix, as though the smoke is orbiting the double helix
asks.summary: Asked for an orbiting particle veil around the scroll form — coherent and streaming while the scroll is driven, turbulent and wandering once it is let go.
asks.effect: A new asset, Veil. The two-state behaviour is the whole spec and it is the part that had never been attempted here: everything before this was either always-moving or driven-only, never a form that changes character depending on whether it is being pushed.

asks.verbatim: it reads as fine dust. So lets treat it as fine dust. Lets make some of the particles, occasionally sparkle, as if they are randomly catching light. And, lets fix the light for the entire thing, the double helix, the particles, everything, looks pretty flat. Lets say the light is coming from above, and it should reflect off the helixes as if it is coming from above, and the light should respect the contours of the shapes
asks.summary: Judged the veil as dust rather than smoke and reclassified it deliberately, then called the whole scene flat and asked for a single light from above that the whole form responds to.
asks.effect: The veil became Dust, with a sparkle. And a proper lighting pass: one shared direction driving the environment, a real lamp, the glass core's shading and both particle systems. The flatness was not a material problem — it was four things lit four different ways.

asks.verbatim: hexagons that are flat and they also orbit the double helix, but they flip slowly and when their faces catch the light they shine irridecent and the flipping should almost behave like snow falling, slow, and random, and there shouldn't be many of them, but they should be larger than the dust by quite a bit. and they behave the same way as the dust and they obey the lighting pattern
asks.summary: Asked for a third, rarer, much larger element in the sheath: flat hexagonal plates that tumble like falling snow and flash iridescent when a face catches the light.
asks.effect: Flakes. Also forced the orbital motion out into a shared module — 'they behave the same way as the dust' is a requirement that two hand-kept copies would quietly break.

asks.verbatim: One of the examples i saw was brighter than the other... i liked the brighter one more
asks.summary: Picked the deliberately over-driven test render over the tuned default, which surfaced a real flaw in how the plates were coloured rather than just a preference for brighter.
asks.effect: Hue and flash were decoupled. The plates now carry iridescence all the time and catching the light adds brightness on top, instead of the flash being the only source of colour.

asks.verbatim: But first, back up what we have so that we dont lose it as we work forward
asks.summary: Asked for a restore point before the next piece of work began.
asks.effect: A tagged checkpoint with three independent copies — an annotated tag and release on the remote, and a full-history bundle plus a worktree archive kept locally. Both local copies were verified by restoring them and diffing, not just written.

asks.verbatim: They need to be larger, and look like glass panels, with depth and texture, while being mostly transparent, but also reflective and they should overlay a protion of the double helix, but not entirely. I like how some are on top and some are on bottom, but they need to stand out as forground with the exception that the hexes may occasionally pass in front of them
asks.summary: Asked for the navigation cards to become large glass panels standing forward of the form, overlapping it without hiding it, with the flakes still able to cross in front.
asks.effect: Panels. Kept the cards as real DOM anchors and put the glass behind them, so the accessibility result this example produced was not traded away for a material.

asks.verbatim: this deserves its on actual page in the gthub repo, its own reachable html so my nephew can see it from his computer. We are obviously not finished with it, but this is a good sharing point
asks.summary: Asked for the study to be reachable from someone else's computer. It already was — the useful part was that it was not yet fit to be looked at by anyone who had not built it.
asks.effect: The page was already live and had been since the first push. What it lacked was share-readiness: it greeted a visitor with a tuning panel, gave no sign the page moved sideways, and unfurled as a bare link with no picture. All three fixed.

asks.verbatim: Make sure the living-page for this project isnt being confused by previous projects. Every time I ask for a living page, it is for it own specific project. The cards link to that page, it appears, and it looks like that has gotten a little blurry with the previous project. Make sure this projects living-page is only about this project.
asks.summary: Caught this page failing to say which project it belongs to, next to another project's page built in the same format.
asks.effect: The page leads with the project's own name instead of the name of a kind of document, and the checker now fails the build if a future one doesn't. A card also links here directly rather than by way of the index.

asks.verbatim: is it possible to make the glass cards play videos, but, like, videos that look like they remain behind the fogged glass. sort of distant? And that project their light through the glass with god rays?
asks.summary: Asked for footage behind the panels, kept distant and diffused by the glass, throwing light forward through it.
asks.effect: Screens and beams. The diffusion turned out to be free — the panel was already frosted and its transmission pass blurs whatever sits behind it — so the work was almost entirely in the light, not the video.

asks.verbatim: is it possible to have each card play a different video? And even better, are there and open source loops we could use, of like, cartoons or something? ... and if the videos could be somewhat transparent so you can still see the background stuff through them
asks.summary: One clip per card, from open-licensed animation, translucent enough to keep the scene visible behind them.
asks.effect: Five loops cut from the Blender Foundation's open movies, one per panel, each with its own decoder that only runs when the camera is near it. The transparency answer was not the one that sounded right.

asks.verbatim: You dont want to over cook any single page, so the home page is probably full enough with different design effects. The next step, which will require some thought, is making linked pages that extend the narrative that the homepage is developing.
asks.summary: Called this page finished for effects and named the next problem as narrative across linked pages rather than more technique on one.
asks.effect: A deliberate stop. Nothing was added in response to this — the direction is that the answer to 'what next' is no longer a rendering question, and the page transition is the first thing that has to be decided.

asks.verbatim: The only issue left with this is that it doesnt fit the screen well. It actually looks great on the phone, when in vertical, but it doesnt fit horizontal on the phone and it doesnt fit well on a monitor.
asks.summary: Reported the framing failing on every landscape screen, with screenshots from real hardware, while portrait reads well.
asks.effect: The camera now fits both axes instead of only width. The reported symptom was the whole bug: fitting a width alone leaves the vertical extent to fall out of the aspect ratio, and nothing ever checked the content still fit.

lessons.lesson: Glass shows you what is behind it, and against a black background that is nothing.
lessons.detail: A transmission sphere over a dark interior absorbs everything — the first Ocellus was almost entirely black. The fix was making the iris emit its own light and thinning the orb, not adding more lights.

lessons.lesson: Lighting and post belong to the asset, not to the page.
lessons.detail: The four-panel rig that flatters the Knot ruined the eye: big rectangular lightformers reflect off a sphere as literal grey rectangles and read as CG instantly. Separately, a bloom threshold that keeps glass clean swallows emissive particles entirely. Two different assets, same conclusion — which is why it became rule R-02.

lessons.lesson: Never nest transmission passes.
lessons.detail: Each transmission material forces its own full-scene render. Putting one inside another's pass tanked the frame hard enough that headless screenshots timed out. Clearcoat and iridescence read as glass perfectly well when something in front is doing the real refracting.

lessons.lesson: Particles alone read as dust. Liquid needs a luminous body.
lessons.detail: Five versions. Bright and dense it swamped the glass and looked like glowing rope; small and sparse it looked like dirt in a tube. The fix was structural, not numeric — a dimmer inner tube of additive colour with the points riding on top as detail. Worth noting that four rounds of tuning numbers preceded the one structural change that worked.

lessons.lesson: Hard refraction turns points into stripes.
lessons.detail: At ior 1.44 the tube facets bent the particles behind them into diagonal bands that read as scales on a snake. Glass that refracts hard is beautiful over an empty background and ruinous over something you actually want to see through it.

lessons.lesson: Leva persists control values by path, not by component lifetime.
lessons.detail: Remounting a component does not reset its values, so per-asset defaults silently did nothing until the control folders were scoped per asset. Applies to any future asset switcher.

lessons.lesson: Anything randomly placed gets a seeded PRNG.
lessons.detail: An asset that rolls a different arrangement on every refresh cannot be art-directed — you would be tuning something that will not exist on the next reload. Determinism is a prerequisite for taste, not a nicety.

lessons.lesson: Alive at rest, surges when pushed — a one-line difference with a large perceptual one.
lessons.detail: flow += delta * (drift + |scrollVelocity| * surge). Drift is never zero, so the page keeps breathing when the user stops. Tie the motion to scroll alone and the page dies in their hands the moment they stop moving.

lessons.lesson: Cards should be real DOM anchors over the canvas, not geometry inside it.
lessons.detail: Real <a> elements positioned by projecting world coordinates to screen pixels each frame. Keyboard-navigable, screen-reader-readable, indexable, and browser-rendered text simply looks better than text in a texture. Opacity, pointer-events and tabIndex all follow camera distance, so a faded card is not a click or tab target.

lessons.lesson: Decoupling scroll from pixels works exactly as intended.
lessons.detail: The span is set in viewport units, so the journey is the same length everywhere. Measured 7700/1100 on desktop and 2940/420 on a phone — identical 7.00 viewport-widths. A phone and an ultrawide travel the same distance at different scales.

lessons.lesson: Fitting a fixed world-width to the frame is NOT enough, and this was the real finding.
lessons.detail: The textbook answer — compute camera distance so a chosen world-width always fits — is right on desktop and wrong on portrait, where it retreats until the form is a thread floating in empty space. Technically correct framing, visually dead. Scaling the visible span with aspect as well takes it from broken to acceptable, not to good. The honest fix is a rotated vertical variant designed as its own composition, and it has not been built.

lessons.lesson: A full-screen scroll proxy must come before the interactive layers, and its wheel listener belongs on window.
lessons.detail: In the first version the proxy sat over the cards and swallowed every click. With the listener on the scroller instead of window, scrolling stopped working whenever the cursor was over a card.

lessons.lesson: Framerate cannot be measured from the build environment, so it is not measured at all here.
lessons.detail: The browser these pages are built through renders on the CPU. Any framerate it reported would be meaningless. Every performance change in this log is an arithmetic reduction in work — fewer pixels, fewer passes — not an observed gain. The live stats panel running on a real GPU is the only evidence, and nobody has read it out yet.

lessons.lesson: Geometry rebuilt in useMemo leaks unless the previous buffer is disposed.
lessons.detail: The merged tube geometries were rebuilt on every parameter change and never freed, so dragging a slider leaked GPU memory until the tab closed. Found incidentally during the perf pass, which is usually how this kind of thing surfaces.

lessons.lesson: “Very small” in world units became sub-pixel on screen, and a sub-pixel point is not a small particle — it is a hard dot.
lessons.detail: The first size default put every particle at roughly a quarter of a pixel. WebGL clamps a point to one pixel, so the soft falloff written into the fragment shader never got to run at all and the veil rendered as a starfield. The fix was arithmetic, not taste: work out the on-screen pixel size at the camera distance the scene actually uses before choosing the default. Small has to mean small against the form, not smaller than a pixel.

lessons.lesson: A peaked alpha falloff plus a bloom threshold turns a particle field into a sparkle field.
lessons.detail: Cubing the falloff concentrated nearly all the alpha into the middle few pixels of each sprite. Individually those centres cleared the bloom threshold and got picked out as points of light, which is the opposite of smoke. A broad flat gaussian keeps every particle under the threshold on its own and only brightens where several overlap — accumulation is what reads as smoke, not the individual sprite.

lessons.lesson: Clearance around a swept form has to be measured from its surface, not its centreline.
lessons.detail: The veil's inner radius was set as a multiple of the helix radius, which is the centreline of the sweep. The tube has a thickness of its own, so at the default the veil's floor sat 0.13 units inside the glass wall it was supposed to be orbiting outside of. Then a second bug compounded it: the billow term scaled the radius, so noise could push a particle a further 22% inward. Nothing about either was visible in a still frame.

lessons.lesson: Re-running a vertex shader on the CPU catches the geometry bugs a screenshot structurally cannot.
lessons.detail: Orbit, containment and wrap are claims about motion and about the whole population. A still frame shows one instant of a few thousand visible particles, so it cannot falsify any of them. Replicating the shader in about eighty lines and asserting the properties directly — minimum radius clears the glass, both spin directions exist, nothing escapes the span at any scroll distance, the axial distribution stays even — found two real bugs that had already survived four rounds of looking at pictures.

lessons.lesson: Four things lit four different ways average out to no light at all.
lessons.detail: The scene looked flat and the instinct was to reach for the glass material. The glass was not the problem. The environment had its own rig, the luminous core was unlit, and both particle systems were flat colour with no notion of a light — and the particles cover most of the form. Nothing agreed about where the light was, so nothing read as lit. The fix was one shared direction, exported from one file, consumed by everything that draws a pixel. Lighting is a property of the scene, not of a material.

lessons.lesson: A fill light at half the key's strength is what flatness is made of.
lessons.detail: The original rig lit the form from above at 4.5 and from below at 2.2. With both sides lit there is no dark side, and without a dark side there is no shape — no amount of work on the surface recovers from it. The bounce is now weak and cold: enough that the underside does not read as a hole punched in the form, not enough to compete with the key. It is the single knob that decides whether the thing reads as lit or as merely glowing.

lessons.lesson: Shading a particle field costs one dot product and does more for form than any material setting.
lessons.detail: Each particle already knows its own direction out from the form's central axis — the flow inside the tube had that vector sitting in a variable, unused. One half-lambert against the shared light direction turns 62k flat specks into a surface that has a top and a bottom. Particles are usually treated as an effect layered over the form; at this density they ARE the form, and lighting them is the cheapest structural improvement available.

lessons.lesson: A convincing sparkle needs a where and a when, multiplied.
lessons.detail: Flickering particles on a timer reads as the whole field blinking. Splitting it in two fixes it: a half-vector term decides WHERE a glint is geometrically possible, and a per-particle flicker decides WHEN it fires. Multiplied, glints cluster in the band actually facing the light and only a fraction fire at once — measured at ~98 of 40,000 at any instant, all of them on the lit side. Only 14% of motes are reflective at all, and a glinting mote also grows slightly, which turns out to be most of what sells it.

lessons.lesson: A sprite can only brighten. Give a particle a face and it can turn away.
lessons.detail: Point sprites are always square-on to the camera, so the only thing they can express is intensity. The moment the ask involved catching light on a face, they stopped being the right primitive — a flat plate is real instanced geometry with an orientation, and orientation is what lets it flash, sweep colour, and then vanish edge-on. The edge-on disappearance costs one dot product against the view direction and does more for the falling-snow read than the tumble maths itself.

lessons.lesson: 'Behaves the same as X' is a requirement to share the code, not to copy it.
lessons.detail: Two systems were meant to ride identical motion. Copying the shader would have satisfied that on day one and broken it the first time either was tuned — and the breakage would be invisible, because nothing fails, the two just quietly stop agreeing. The motion moved into one module that both shaders paste in and both components drive through one update function. Sameness became structural rather than remembered, which is the same principle the generated log itself runs on.

lessons.lesson: Building a basis from a normal collapses when the normal meets the reference vector.
lessons.detail: A tumbling plate needs a local basis, and the obvious cross(up, normal) goes to zero every time the plate points straight up — once per tumble, per plate, forever. The fix is to swap the reference vector when the normal gets near vertical. Checked rather than assumed: the smallest cross product over 400 simulated seconds is 0.31, so the basis never gets close to degenerate.

lessons.lesson: Two incommensurate rates read as random; one rate reads as machinery.
lessons.detail: The tumble is two angles advancing at unrelated per-plate rates, plus a slow flutter term. Because the rates never share a period, the motion has no visible loop — which is most of what 'random' means to an eye watching for a few seconds. Measured: a full turn takes about 38 seconds and the fastest plate tumbles 12x the slowest. Snow is slower than instinct suggests; the first guess was several times too fast.

lessons.lesson: When a taste call points at an over-driven test render, find what it is actually pointing at.
lessons.detail: A render made purely to prove a mechanism was preferred to the tuned default. Taking that literally would have meant widening the flash until every plate flashed constantly — which buys the colour back by destroying the event the flash exists to represent. The real fault was underneath: hue was driven by the flash, so a plate not currently catching the light had no colour at all and the field sat grey between flashes. Separating the two gives the brightness that was actually wanted and keeps the behaviour that was asked for a message earlier. A preference between two pictures is evidence about the pictures, not an instruction about the parameters that produced them.

lessons.lesson: Clear glass on a dark background is invisible, because there is nothing for it to reflect.
lessons.detail: The first panel was physically correct — transmission 1, low roughness, real thickness — and could only be located by the smear it made of the form behind it. A debug pass with an opaque material proved it was exactly where it should be, the right size, correctly aligned with its label. The material was not wrong; the environment gave it nothing to return. A real panel is found by its edges first, so the edge is now drawn as its own geometry rather than left to the material to imply, and the face is frosted enough to scatter the key across itself instead of returning it at one angle.

lessons.lesson: When a material change threatens an earlier result, put the material behind it rather than in place of it.
lessons.detail: The cards were the thing this example proved: real DOM anchors, keyboard-navigable, screen-reader-readable, browser-rendered text, positioned from world space. Glass with real refraction can only come from WebGL. Rebuilding the cards in WebGL would have bought the material by giving back the finding. Putting the panel in the scene and leaving the text in the DOM on top of it keeps both, at one stated cost: the flakes cross in front of the glass but never in front of the type.

lessons.lesson: A backup that has not been restored from is a claim, not a backup.
lessons.detail: The bundle was checked by cloning from it into a scratch directory and comparing tree hashes against the live repo; the archive by extracting it and diffing against the working tree. Both matched. That is a different statement from 'the file was written and is 483K'. Worth the two extra commands every time — and the restore notes record the one confusing detail, that git bundle verify has to run from inside a repo and reports a bad-bundle-looking error from anywhere else.

lessons.lesson: Shipped and shareable are different states, and it is easy to mistake the first for the second.
lessons.detail: The page had been publicly reachable from the first push. What it was not was fit for a stranger: the first thing a visitor met was a developer's tuning panel, nothing on screen said the page moved sideways so a still-looking picture was a plausible read, and a shared link unfurled with no image. None of that shows up while building, because the person building it already knows how it works and has the panel open on purpose.

lessons.lesson: A negative result from a selector nobody checked is not a result.
lessons.detail: The tuning panel was confirmed hidden in the production build by querying an element id the library does not use — so the check returned 'absent' for a panel that might have been sitting there in plain sight. The same wrong selector then reported the panel missing when it was demonstrably present, which is what exposed it. Any check that can only come back negative proves nothing; make it succeed once against a case you know is positive before trusting it against the case you care about.

lessons.lesson: Being unable to use a name is not a reason to have none.
lessons.detail: This page is published from a public repo and the project's own name has to stay off it, so it was titled 'Asset Log' — a kind of document, not a project. Every word of its content was its own and its only outbound link was its own repo, but a title that would fit any other project unchanged identifies nothing, and beside another project's page in the same format it read as a generic sibling of it. The restriction was on one particular name, not on having one; the public repo name was available the whole time and is already findable. The heading now carries the project and the document type is demoted to a kicker above it.

lessons.lesson: When a material already does a thing, put the content where the material can act on it.
lessons.detail: 'Behind fogged glass, sort of distant' sounds like a video treatment — blur it, desaturate it, dim it. None of that was needed. The panel is frosted and its transmission pass already blurs whatever is behind it, so a plane placed behind the glass comes out diffused by the material itself, and how far back it sits is the entire distance control. A blur applied to the video would have been an effect that has to be kept in sync with the glass by hand; this one cannot go out of sync because it is the same physics.

lessons.lesson: A rim term draws a shell's own outline. It is right for atmospheres and wrong for beams.
lessons.detail: The first beam was a hollow frustum whose alpha rose where the surface turned edge-on — the standard trick for a glow around a sphere, where the eye really does see through more material at the limb. On an open cone it puts maximum brightness exactly along the silhouette, so it drew two hard diagonal lines across the frame: a picture of the geometry rather than of light. Replaced with a stack of soft slices along the beam axis, where the edge fade is explicit instead of inferred from the viewing angle.

lessons.lesson: A beam aimed at the camera is a rectangle, and an unbroken source is a wash.
lessons.detail: Two separate reasons the first attempts did not look like god rays. The light leaves the panel travelling toward the viewer, and a beam seen down its own axis has no length to show — it needed raking, which the scene's own light direction supplied, since light leaves a window travelling away from whatever lit it. And a plain rectangle emits evenly: rays are only legible because something breaks the source up. Adding striation at two incommensurate frequencies was the difference between a glow and a beam.

lessons.lesson: One decoder, many surfaces.
lessons.detail: Five panels suggests five videos, which is five decoders running at once and the reason a page like this stutters on a laptop. One element feeds every panel and each takes a different crop of the same frame, which costs nothing and stops them reading as five copies of one thing. The element is parked in the document rather than left detached — a detached video decodes in some browsers and quietly does not in others, and display:none is a documented reason to stop decoding altogether.

lessons.lesson: Additive blending makes the dark end transparent and the bright end worthless.
lessons.detail: 'See the background through them' sounds like additive, and for shadow it is exactly right — black contributes nothing, so the form reads straight through. But a bright frame then saturates, the bloom pass finds it, and the panel becomes a lit rectangle with no picture in it. Normal blending under full opacity is see-through everywhere and keeps an image everywhere, which is what was actually wanted. Additive stayed as an option because the holographic read is worth having; it is not the default.

lessons.lesson: A DOM side effect inside useMemo has no cleanup, so it runs twice and leaves one behind.
lessons.detail: Each panel builds a video element and parks it in the document. The append was written inside the useMemo that creates the element, which StrictMode calls twice with nothing in between — so every card left an orphaned element in the page and five cards were quietly running ten decoders. Precisely the cost the one-decoder-per-card design existed to control. Moving the append into an effect, where there is a cleanup to pair it with, fixed it. Counted rather than assumed: five elements, five distinct sources, two of them decoding.

lessons.lesson: Trailers are mostly title cards. Look at the footage before cutting from it.
lessons.detail: Five clips cut from two trailers on plausible-looking timestamps came back as three title cards, a fade to black, and two usable shots. Sampling a frame per second and building a contact sheet showed the actual structure: the source cuts to a title every two or three seconds, so the usable runs are short and have to be found rather than guessed. The loops are seamless by crossfading the tail back onto the head rather than by palindrome — a palindrome is simpler and reads as rewind on character animation, which a rabbit walking backwards makes obvious.

lessons.lesson: A page can be finished for effects long before it is finished.
lessons.detail: Every element here earned its place and the page still reached a point where the next good decision was to stop adding to it. Restraint is not a technical judgement and nothing in this log could have produced it — the effects each worked, none of them was wrong, and one more would still have rendered. It came from the director looking at the whole thing and saying it was full. Worth recording because the failure it avoids leaves no trace: a page that is merely busy looks, from inside the work, exactly like a page that is rich.

lessons.lesson: Fitting one axis means the other is whatever the aspect ratio leaves you.
lessons.detail: The camera distance was solved for a world width, which makes it inversely proportional to the aspect ratio — so the wider the screen the CLOSER the camera comes, and the less vertical world stays in frame. Nothing ever asked whether the content still fit top to bottom. Measured on a 2:1 monitor: 2.02 units of half-height for panels reaching 2.4, clipped by about ninety pixels, with the form taking 72% of the frame. It survived this long because the failure gets worse as screens get wider and the study was built and reviewed at 640x400 and 900x560, which are the two aspects where it very nearly holds.

lessons.lesson: Fitting content to a frame is a question about depth, not just size.
lessons.detail: The panels stand 1.75 units in front of the form, so they are nearer the camera and magnified relative to it — the tallest content in the scene is also the closest, and the two compound. A fit computed against the origin plane is wrong for anything that does not sit on it. The fix asks, for each piece of content, how far back the camera must be for THAT piece at ITS OWN depth, and takes the largest answer. Arithmetic against the origin plane predicted 2.75 units of half-height where the real number was 2.02, and the whole of that gap was depth.

lessons.lesson: The screen the work is reviewed on is a test condition nobody declares.
lessons.detail: Every judgement in this log was made through a 640x400 or 900x560 frame, because that is what the build environment could render. Both sit near the aspect where the framing bug almost does not show. It took a screenshot from a real monitor to surface something that had been shipping wrong on every wide screen for days. Worth stating as a limit of the method rather than a one-off: the review viewport is as much a part of the apparatus as the renderer, and this one had been silently narrowing what could be seen.

perf_levers.why: Cost scales with the square, so 2.0 → 1.5 is 44% fewer pixels shaded.
This material re-renders the whole scene into a buffer every frame; halving the edge is a quarter of the pixels.
Renders the mesh a second time through that pass — the most expensive checkbox on the page.
Full-screen MSAA on every pass. Bloom hides much of what it buys.

open.q: The rotated vertical variant for portrait is still not built.
open.why: The one thing the scroll test genuinely failed. The mitigation in place is acceptable, not good, and everyone involved knows the difference.

open.q: Persistent canvas — the only decision here with a deadline.
open.why: If the WebGL context unmounts between pages you get a white flash and a shader recompile, and the illusion breaks completely. Hiding that seam means one application with a context that never dies and DOM content swapping around it. It cannot be retrofitted, so it has to be decided before anything real is scaffolded. It also settles a second question: whether the linked pages are further WebGL worlds or conventional documents.

open.q: The vehicle is not formally locked.
open.why: Both studies are R3F and it works, so it is the de-facto answer — but vanilla Three (dropping the React overhead for a pure performance showcase) and WebGPU/TSL (newer, rougher, genuinely ahead) were never formally ruled out.

open.q: Nobody has read a framerate off a real GPU yet.
open.why: The stats panel exists in both studies for exactly this. Until someone opens it on real hardware, every performance claim in this log is arithmetic rather than evidence. See L-13.

open.q: Composition is untested — everything here is one object, centred, on black.
open.why: The friendliest possible case, and the premise has only been tested inside it. Multi-element scenes with foreground, midground and background are where procedural work usually starts looking like a shader demo rather than a place.
Text living inside the 3D scene rather than in the DOM layer over it. Different problem from the card anchors, which are solved.

open.q: Whether an articulated form following a spline needs modeling at all.
open.why: Repeated segments instanced along a curve is a procedural strength, not a weakness. It was conceded as needing real geometry and never actually tested — a cheap study, still unbuilt.

open.q: The house-style risk, which is art direction rather than technique.
open.why: Procedural work has a look. A great deal of it is technically extraordinary and completely anonymous — it reads as a shader demo. The gap between that and something that reads as a place built with intent is composition and restraint, and no amount of craft in this log closes it.

open.q: What 40k additional soft additive points cost.
open.why: They are cheap per vertex and the maths is trivial, but they are large soft sprites and the overdraw is real. Same problem as everything else here: it cannot be measured from the build environment, so the count sits on a slider and the stats panel is the only evidence.

open.q: Whether the key is too hot at the default.
open.why: The specular streak reads clearly as light from above, which was the ask, but it blows close to white on the upper faces and the form underneath it is a saturated magenta. That may be exactly right or it may look pasted on — it is a judgement about the picture, and it has only been seen through a CPU-rendered frame at 640x400.

open.q: Whether the flakes want to be scarcer and larger still.
open.why: The brief said rare and much bigger, and the defaults are one reading of that — 220 plates at a size where a couple are catching light in frame at any moment. Twice the size and half the number is a different picture and might be the better one. Only an eye on real hardware can pick.

open.q: The panels do not fade with distance but their labels do.
open.why: The DOM anchors fade with camera distance so they arrive and leave rather than popping. The glass does not — it is scenery and sits in the world permanently. At the frame edges that can mean a visible panel with no text on it. It may read as perfectly natural or as an oversight, and only watching it move will tell.

open.q: What the beams cost, and whether they survive real footage.
open.why: Twenty-two additive slices per panel is a lot of overdraw for something this subtle, and it has never been measured on a GPU. The placeholder is also a slow abstract gradient, which is the kindest possible input — real footage cuts, and a beam colour sampled six times a second across a hard cut may strobe.

open.q: The page transition, which stops being optional the moment there is a second page.
open.why: Clicking a card does a normal page load — the one seam in this study still fully visible, and the only one that cannot be hidden by tuning something. Carrying the world across a navigation needs a WebGL context that outlives the page, with the DOM swapping around it. That is an architecture decision, and it is now the first one, because linked pages are the next piece of work.

open.q: Whether a landscape phone wants this composition at all.
open.why: It fits now, which is not the same as being designed for. A 2.2:1 frame 390 pixels tall gets the form and a panel and very little air, and the honest answer may be a different arrangement rather than a further-back camera — the same argument already made for portrait, from the other end.
